title: Before There Was a Wedding, There Was a Garden: How Ephesians 5 Builds on Genesis 2
paragraphs: Before There Was a Wedding, There Was a Garden: How Ephesians 5 Builds on Genesis 2
Paul’s teaching on marriage did not begin with first-century culture. It reaches backward to Eden, then opens forward into the mystery of Christ and His Church.
Before there was a wedding aisle, there was a garden.

Before there was a pastor asking two people to repeat vows, before rings were exchanged, before photographs, receptions, anniversaries, arguments over money, nights of sleeping inches apart while feeling miles away, and whispered prayers asking God whether a wounded marriage could possibly live again…
there was Eden.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was God.
That matters more than we sometimes realize.
Because when the apostle Paul reaches one of the most profound passages about marriage ever written, he does something extraordinary.
He reaches backward.
All the way back.
Past Rome.
Past Greece.
Past Israel’s kings.
Past Moses at Sinai.
Back to Genesis.
And then Paul takes words spoken about the first husband and wife and reveals something breathtaking hiding within God’s design:
Marriage was never merely about marriage.
It was always pointing beyond itself.
Toward Christ.
Toward His people.
Toward a Bridegroom who would love His bride at unimaginable cost.
That is why understanding Ephesians 5 without Genesis 2 is like walking into the middle of a conversation and assuming you heard the beginning.
You did not.
Paul himself gives us the bridge.
After describing the love of a husband for his wife, he writes:
Then comes the quotation:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.”
That is Ephesians 5:31, drawing directly from Genesis 2:24.
Paul deliberately brings Eden into his argument.
And immediately afterward he says:
“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
Ephesians 5:32.
Stop there.
Read it again slowly.
Paul has just quoted the creation account of marriage, and then he speaks about Christ and the Church.
This is not Paul randomly attaching Jesus to an unrelated marriage text.
He is showing us how the biblical story fits together.
To understand what he is doing, we have to return to the garden.
Genesis 2:18 records something startling.
After repeatedly declaring His creation good, God says:
“It is not good that the man should be alone.”
In Hebrew:
לֹא־טוֹב הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ
Lo-tov heyot ha’adam levado.
“It is not good for the man to be alone.”
God then declares:
אֶעֱשֶׂה־לּוֹ עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ
E‘eseh-lo ‘ezer kenegdo.
“I will make for him a helper corresponding to him.”
That final expression matters.
כְּנֶגְדּוֹ — kenegdo — carries the sense of one corresponding to him, suitable for him, standing in relation to him.
And עֵזֶר — ‘ezer, “helper” — is not inherently a degrading word.
Scripture can use ‘ezer for God Himself as the help of His people.
The woman is therefore not introduced as an inferior accessory to the man.
She is the human counterpart he did not find among the creatures.
Then God does what Adam could never accomplish for himself.
God provides.
The man sleeps.
God acts.
God forms the woman and brings her to the man.
And when Adam sees her, Scripture records the first human words spoken in the Bible:
“This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
You can almost hear the recognition.
At last.
Here is someone like me.
Someone corresponding to me.
Someone with whom human life can be shared in covenant union.
Then Genesis gives us the foundational statement:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד
basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Not merely two people sharing an address.
Not merely romantic attraction.
Not merely sexual desire.
Scripture describes a profound union in which husband and wife are joined together in the marriage bond.
Jesus Himself later returns to this very passage.
In Matthew 19, when questioned about divorce, Christ points His hearers beyond their arguments and back toward creation.
He quotes Genesis and concludes:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Jesus treats Genesis 2 as foundational for understanding marriage.
Paul does the same.
But in Ephesians 5, another dimension becomes explicit.
Paul takes the “one flesh” language of Genesis and places it beside Christ’s relationship with His Church.
And suddenly the garden begins to look toward the Gospel.
Paul writes:
The Greek is striking:
ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς
ho Christos ēgapēsen tēn ekklēsian kai heauton paredōken hyper autēs.
“Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Notice where Paul puts the weight.
Christ loved.
Christ gave Himself.
That means biblical marital love cannot be reduced to domination, entitlement, convenience, or getting another person to satisfy you.
The model Paul places before the husband is Jesus Christ.
And what did Jesus do?
He gave Himself.
That changes everything.
Because sinful humanity naturally asks:
“What am I getting from this relationship?”
Christlike love asks:
“How can I faithfully give myself for the good of the one God has entrusted to me?”
This does not mean enabling abuse, pretending sin does not matter, or removing wise and necessary boundaries. Christlike love is holy love. Scripture never requires evil to be renamed as goodness.
But Ephesians destroys the idea that biblical headship gives a husband permission to become a selfish tyrant.
Paul does not point husbands toward Caesar.
He points them toward a crucified Savior.
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
That is not permission to exploit.
It is a summons to self-giving love.
And the surrounding passage begins with an instruction Christians sometimes rush past:
“Submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.”
Ephesians 5:21.
Everything that follows belongs within a Christian life being transformed by the Spirit and ordered under the lordship of Jesus.
This is not primarily a technique for winning arguments between husbands and wives.
It is discipleship.
It is about what happens when Jesus enters the center of human relationships and begins confronting our pride, selfishness, fear, resentment, lust, bitterness, and hunger for control.
And that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because Genesis 2 gives us the beauty.
Genesis 3 gives us the fracture.
The man and woman who had been naked and unashamed hide.
Sin enters.
Blame enters.
Fear enters.
Alienation enters.
The relationship between humanity and God fractures, and human relationships begin experiencing the consequences.
We still live in that world.
Some people reading this grew up watching a marriage collapse.
Some watched their father wound their mother.
Some watched their mother wound their father.
Some learned to associate marriage with shouting, betrayal, manipulation, abandonment, silence, or fear.
Some promised themselves:
“I will never become like them.”
Then years passed.
And one frightening day you heard their words coming out of your mouth.
You recognized their anger in your anger.
Their coldness in your silence.
Their selfishness in your choices.
Their wounds living inside your reactions.
And perhaps nobody knows.
Your Facebook photographs look fine.
Your family thinks you are fine.
People at church shake your hand and think you are fine.
You might even serve in ministry.
But there are rooms inside your heart where something is dying.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than religious vocabulary.
Because Christianity does not teach that humanity simply needs better relationship advice.
Our problem goes deeper.
Sin has reached into the human heart.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness.
We need new hearts.
We need grace.
We need Jesus.
And this is why Ephesians 5 becomes so breathtaking when read against Genesis 2.
The first marriage takes place before the fall.
But Paul writes from the other side of humanity’s rebellion and points toward the One who came to redeem sinners.
Christ does not love a flawless bride.
He gives Himself for a people who need cleansing.
Paul writes that Christ gave Himself for the Church “that he might sanctify her.”
Think about what that means.
Jesus did not wait until His people became beautiful enough to deserve the cross.
The cross is where undeserving sinners encounter the astonishing love and grace of God.
Romans tells us that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
This is not sentimental love.
It is costly love.
Holy love.
Saving love.
Love with scars in its hands.
And perhaps this is the sentence someone desperately needs tonight:
Jesus is not intimidated by the part of your story you are ashamed to tell.
Your sin must not be excused.
Your betrayal should not be renamed.
Your pride should not be defended.
Your hidden lust should not be protected.
Your cruelty should not be spiritualized.
Your bitterness should not become your permanent home.
Repentance is real.
Consequences can be real.
Reconciliation between people may require truth, safety, wisdom, time, accountability, and genuine change.
But shame does not get the final word over the person who comes to Christ.
Jesus does.
That is the movement from scandal to grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not calling darkness light.
Not hiding what sin destroyed.
Grace looks directly at the wreckage and declares that the blood of Jesus is greater than the sinner’s past.
That does not make sin small.
The cross proves sin is devastatingly serious.
But the cross also proves grace is astonishingly great.
This is why Ephesians 5 does more than give married people instructions.
It reveals a Gospel-shaped vision of covenant love.
Paul tells husbands to love their wives as their own bodies:
“He who loves his wife loves himself.”
Why?
Again, Genesis is underneath the argument.
“One flesh.”
The wife is not an opponent to defeat.
The husband is not supposed to behave as though his wife’s flourishing is irrelevant to his own.
Paul continues:
“For no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church.”
The Greek verbs are vivid.
ἐκτρέφει — ektrephei — carries the idea of nourishing or bringing up.
θάλπει — thalpei — conveys tender care or cherishing.
And again Paul brings us back to Jesus.
“Just as Christ does the church.”
Christ remains the center.
Not masculinity as culture defines it.
Not femininity as culture defines it.
Not the husband’s ego.
Not the wife’s ego.
Christ.
This is where Christian marriage becomes radically different from a contract built merely around mutual satisfaction.
A consumer relationship says:
“I remain as long as you keep giving me what I purchased.”
Covenant speaks a different language.
And yet Christian covenant is never permission for one spouse to weaponize Scripture against the other.
A husband cannot quote “wives, submit” while conveniently forgetting “Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
A wife cannot use her husband’s failures as permission to abandon Christlike character.
Neither spouse gets to make themselves Jesus.
Both stand beneath His authority.
Both need His grace.
Both are sinners.
Both are accountable to God.
And neither is the other’s Savior.
That last truth can save people from enormous disappointment.
Your spouse cannot carry the weight of being your Messiah.
No husband can satisfy the deepest hunger of the human soul.
No wife can heal the fundamental separation between humanity and God.
Marriage is precious.
But marriage is not Christ.
In fact, Paul’s argument eventually lifts our eyes beyond marriage itself.
“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
The Greek reads:
τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν
to mystērion touto mega estin.
“This mystery is great/profound.”
The word μυστήριον — mystērion — in Paul does not mean a puzzle that clever people can solve.
It often describes something in God’s redemptive purpose that has now been disclosed.
Paul sees something magnificent in Genesis 2.
The “one flesh” union of husband and wife has a correspondence to the relationship between Christ and His Church.
Marriage therefore points beyond itself.
Every Christian marriage is temporary in its earthly form.
Jesus teaches that in the resurrection people “neither marry nor are given in marriage.”
Why?
Because earthly marriage is not the final destination of redemption.
Christ is.
The Church is heading toward the wedding feast of the Lamb.
The Bible begins with a marriage in a garden and moves toward the marriage supper of the Lamb in Revelation.
And between those scenes stands a cross.
A Bridegroom gives Himself for His bride.
This is where the Bible’s story becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
Genesis gives us a bride brought to a man.
The Gospel gives us a Savior who gives His life to redeem His people.
Genesis gives us one flesh.
Ephesians reveals Christ and the Church.
Genesis gives us nakedness without shame.
Sin gives humanity hiding.
The Gospel gives sinners a place to stop hiding because forgiveness has been purchased by Christ.
Do you see why this matters beyond marriage?
You might be single.
Widowed.
Divorced.
Abandoned.
Never married.
You might desperately desire marriage.
You might carry scars from one that failed.
Ephesians 5 still has something enormous to tell you.
Your ultimate hope is not found in getting married.
Your ultimate hope is Jesus Christ.
Marriage can point toward Him.
It cannot replace Him.
And perhaps that is why some of us are so exhausted.
We have been asking human beings to do what only Jesus can do.
“Make me whole.”
“Tell me I matter.”
“Never disappoint me.”
“Never leave me emotionally empty.”
“Carry all my wounds.”
“Give my life meaning.”
No human being can survive being made into another person’s god.
But Christ can carry what your spouse cannot.
Christ can forgive what you cannot erase.
Christ can expose what you have spent years hiding and still call you toward Himself.
Christ can take the person who says, “I destroyed everything,” and begin the long, holy work of repentance and transformation.
That does not guarantee every broken earthly relationship will be restored exactly as we desire.
The Bible gives us no license to promise that.
But it gives us something even deeper.
A Redeemer.
Maybe your marriage needs counseling.
Get wise, biblically faithful help.
Maybe you need to confess something you have hidden.
Bring darkness into the light with appropriate wisdom and accountability.
Maybe abuse or danger is present.
Seeking safety and qualified help is not spiritual failure.
Maybe your marriage is healthy but drifting into complacency.
Return to Christ before distance becomes a canyon.
Maybe you are unmarried and wondering whether your life is somehow incomplete.
Do not let a wedding become your functional savior.
Jesus was not married, and He lived the fullest human life ever lived.
The Church desperately needs a theology of marriage beautiful enough to honor marriage without turning it into an idol.
Genesis 2 and Ephesians 5 give us exactly that.
Marriage matters enormously.
But Christ matters infinitely more.
And here is the question I cannot answer for you:
If your relationships revealed exactly how deeply you believe the Gospel, what would they say?
Would they reveal grace?
Repentance?
Truth?
Sacrifice?
Forgiveness?
Or would they expose the secret kingdom you have been building around yourself?
Maybe this article is not really about somebody else’s marriage.
Maybe God is putting His finger on you.
The apology you keep refusing to give.
The pornography you keep deleting from your history but not from your life.
The bitterness you rehearse every night.
The emotional affair you insist is “just friendship.”
The contempt hidden underneath your jokes.
The pride that needs to win every argument.
The wound you refuse to bring into the light.
The spiritual performance that keeps everybody convinced you are okay.
You can hide from people.
You cannot hide from Christ.
And strangely, terrifyingly, beautifully…
that is good news.
Because the One who sees everything is also the One who went to the cross for sinners.
Repentance is not running away from grace.
It is turning toward the God of grace.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself up enough and maybe Jesus will want you.”
The Gospel announces that Christ died and rose, and sinners are summoned to repent and believe in Him.
You do not need a better mask.
You need a Savior.
And when Jesus becomes the center, He does not merely decorate the old life with religious language.
He begins making people new.
That is what makes the Christian story so scandalous.
Peter could fail.
Paul could have blood on his history.
The thief beside Jesus could have nothing left to offer.
Sinners could come out of darkness.
Prodigals could come home.
Not because sin did not matter.
Because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be honest before God.
If you need mercy, comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
If you are exhausted but refuse to abandon your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to remember you in prayer, comment, “pray for me.”
If God is healing places you once thought would remain broken forever, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
And if you are tired of performing Christianity while hiding the real battle, comment, “no more hiding.”
Not because typing words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes honesty begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
And somebody reading the comments may discover they were never fighting alone.
And yes, send it even to the person who does not yet believe.
One shared article cannot save a soul.
But the Gospel it points toward is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.
Because there may come a night when love feels less like a wedding photograph and more like carrying a cross, and you will need to remember:
Christian marriage was never supposed to survive on romance alone.
It must keep returning to Christ.
We want this community to remain a place for daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, repentance, grace, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and one way those who value this particular work can help it continue is by supporting and sharing it.
We are not.
Jesus is.
Genesis 2 begins with God joining a man and woman.
Ephesians 5 reaches into that ancient union and shows us something larger.
Christ loves His Church.
Christ gave Himself for her.
Christ nourishes and cherishes His people.
Christ sanctifies.
Christ cleanses.
Christ saves.
And one day every marriage photograph will fade.
Every wedding ring will eventually leave somebody’s hand.
Every earthly love story will reach its final page.
But the Bridegroom who conquered death will still be standing.
So when your marriage is beautiful, let it point to Him.
When your marriage is struggling, run toward Him.
When you are single, find your deepest identity in Him.
When you have sinned, repent and come to Him.
When shame tells you the story is over, remember the cross.
When grace seems impossible, remember the empty tomb.
Because the deepest promise hidden beneath this entire story is not that every earthly romance gets the ending we imagined.
It is that Jesus Christ is still redeeming sinners.
And sometimes the place you thought would become the grave of your story becomes the very place where grace teaches you how desperately you needed the Savior.
Eden showed us what one flesh was meant to be; Calvary showed us how far the Bridegroom would go to bring His people home.
